page: Google Cloud Platform c4a-highcpu-1 is an entry-level virtual machine based on the ARM64 processor architecture. It provides 1 dedicated vCPU alongside 2.0 GB of system memory, establishing a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio characteristic of compute-focused hardware profiles. The instance includes no bundled local storage or hardware accelerators, requiring external network block storage for operating system deployment and runtime persistence. It also does not include complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

The dedicated allocation model guarantees that the single ARM64 virtual core operates without fractional time-slicing or CPU credit exhaustion. However, the limited 2.0 GB memory capacity introduces a strict operational ceiling. Environments requiring high concurrency, memory-mapped databases, or large working sets are structurally constrained by the low memory ceiling and the complete reliance on network storage for disk I/O.

In terms of qualitative cost efficiency, the small resource allocation provides a low-overhead entry point for testing and running ARM64-compatible services. The instance is suited for lightweight microservices, continuous integration build workers, background job processing, network proxies, and small stateless API backends that do not demand extensive memory.
description: Google Cloud Platform c4a-highcpu-1 is a compact ARM64 virtual machine designed for entry-level, compute-oriented tasks. It provides 1 dedicated vCPU paired with 2.0 GB of memory, maintaining a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. The server configuration features no bundled local storage and zero GPU accelerators, relying entirely on network-attached storage for persistent disk access. In addition, no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned. The single dedicated execution core provides consistent processing throughput without shared-core throttling, although the 2.0 GB memory pool bounds the complexity of active processes. This server type is technically aligned with lightweight stateless microservices, background job consumers, utility containers, and development or testing pipelines targeting ARM architectures.
